s: Part one.
The CLAUDE.md hierarchy.
By the end of this part, you'll know where the instruction file can live, how its levels combine, how to split it up, and why no amount of emphasis turns it into a lock.
Let's start with the plain version.
Imagine a whiteboard by the door of a workshop.
It's read aloud at the start of every shift.
Several parties are allowed to write on it.
The organization's IT department can write on it.
You can write on it.
The project you're working on can write on it.
And you can add a private sticky note that only you ever see.
Two things about this whiteboard matter.
First.
Nobody has an eraser.
Everything anyone wrote gets read out, every shift, in a fixed order.
Second.
Reading it out costs attention.
A crowded board buries the lines that matter.
The technical name for that whiteboard is CLAUDE.md.
It's a plain text file of standing instructions.
Claude Code loads it into context before your conversation even starts.
The course video calls it persistent context.
That's a good two-word summary.
And there are several places it can live.
In exam terms, these are scopes.
The study notes, checked against current documentation, name four scopes.
Here they are in load order, from broadest to most specific.
One.
A managed policy file that IT deploys to a protected operating-system location.
Two.
Your user file, at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.
It lives in your home folder, and it applies to every project you open.
Three.
The project file.
It can sit at the repository root as ./CLAUDE.md.
Or inside the .claude folder at the root, as ./.claude/CLAUDE.md.
Those two project locations are equivalent.
Pick whichever your team prefers.
Four.
A local file called CLAUDE.local.md, at the repository root.
It's personal, and it's ignored by version control.
So it is never committed.
Now the first source disagreement you need to know about.
The course video describes three levels.
User, project, and directory.
The notes describe four scopes.
Managed policy, user, project, and local.
And they treat directory files as a loading behavior of the project scope.
Are these in conflict?
Not really.
They slice the same system differently.
The video's third level, a CLAUDE.md inside a subdirectory, is real.
We'll come to it.
So.
If a question lists three levels, answer in its terms.
If it mentions managed policy or the local file, you now know where they sit.
How do these files load?
Claude Code starts from the folder you launched it in.
It walks up the tree.
And it loads every CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md it finds, stitching them together from the top of the filesystem down toward your working folder.
In each folder, the local file is appended after the regular one.
And files in subfolders below where you started?
They don't load at launch.
They load on demand, the first time Claude reads a file in that subfolder.
Quick recap before the first question.
Four scopes.
Stitched together from the top down.
Subfolder files wait until they're needed.
Question one.
Practice question D3-001.
The course presenter flagged this scenario directly as an exam question.
Here's the scenario.
A teammate isn't getting the conventions.
Claude works perfectly for one person, and acts as if it has never heard of the project for another.
The conventions live in the lead's user file, in his home folder.
A contractor cloned the repository last week, and Claude ignores them.
The stem adds a constraint.
The fix must reach every contributor, and the continuous integration job, which is the automated build that runs on a server.
And it must work without any per-machine setup.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
The presenter's advice was blunt: check the config location first.
Then move the conventions into the project CLAUDE.md, and commit it.
Here's the plain version.
It's like pinning the house rules to your own bedroom door instead of the fridge.
You see them every day, so they feel shared.
But your new flatmate never walks into your room.
Move the note to the fridge, where everyone looks, and the problem disappears.
In exam terms, version control is the distribution mechanism.
Every clone, and every pipeline checkout, gets the file on pull.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: ask the contractor to copy the file into her own home folder, and keep the copies in sync.
Why?
It fails the no-per-machine-setup constraint.
It drifts as the conventions change.
And it never reaches the build server.
Wrong: put the conventions in CLAUDE.local.md, beside the code.
Why?
It sounds shared, because it sits in the repository folder.
But the local file is the personal, ignored scope.
It's never committed.
So neither the contractor nor the pipeline gets it.
Wrong: add an import line in the lead's user file, pointing at a conventions file inside the repository.
This is the cleverest distractor.
Why is it wrong?
The import sits in a file only the lead has.
Anyone without that file never follows the import.
Listen for three constraint words.
Every contributor.
The pipeline.
No per-machine setup.
Those three together mean project scope, committed.
Hold on to this line.
User scope is never shared.
So when a teammate is missing the conventions, check where the file lives.
Now the second big idea in this part.
And it's the one the exam leans on hardest.
Remember the whiteboard with no eraser?
The scopes are additive.
They do not override each other.
All discovered content lands in context at once.
And when two instructions contradict each other, Claude reconciles them by judgment, turn by turn.
Question two.
Practice question D3-002.
Here's the scenario.
A developer's user file says: write commit messages as a single imperative sentence.
The project file says: use Conventional Commits.
That's a structured format with a type, a scope in brackets, and a summary.
Claude follows one format on some commits, and the other format on others.
The developer wants the project rule to hold in this repository, without changing their other repositories.
What should they do?
Take a second.
The answer.
Delete the commit-format line from the user file.
And keep user scope for preferences a project will not contradict.
A commit format is a project decision.
Here's the plain version.
Two notes on the same fridge.
Yours says buy oat milk.
The household's says buy dairy milk.
Whoever shops has to guess, and they guess differently each week.
Writing the household note bigger doesn't settle it.
Taking your note down does.
The notes put it memorably.
Hold on to this line.
If your user file says always use one package manager, and the project file says another, you have not configured precedence.
You have configured a coin flip.
Now the wrong turns.
They're all attempts to out-rank, rather than remove.
Wrong: move the project rule into ./.claude/CLAUDE.md, because it loads later and therefore wins.
Why?
It's wrong twice.
The two project locations are equivalent.
And load order decides what is read first, never what wins.
Wrong: restate the rule in capitals, with a note that project instructions always override user instructions.
Why?
Emphasis does not create precedence.
Both lines stay in context.
Wrong: copy the project rule into the local file, so it appears twice and outweighs the user line.
Why?
Repetition is not a weighting rule.
The contradiction remains.
And now you pay for the text twice.
A related question from the notes.
A senior engineer's user file says: always run the full test suite.
The project file says: never run the full suite locally, because it takes forty minutes.
And the engineer files a bug saying project scope should override user scope.
What's the accurate assessment?
There are no override semantics to be broken.
Nothing is corrupted.
Remove the contradiction.
And if the behavior must be guaranteed, use a hook.
We'll come to that in a moment.
So remember.
CLAUDE.md scopes are additive.
Fix a contradiction by deleting a line.
Never by moving files, or shouting.
Next, modularity.
Plain version first.
Picture a staff handbook where each department writes its own chapter, in its own document.
The front page simply says: testing, see chapter three.
Everyone still gets the whole handbook on day one.
The only change is that two departments no longer fight over the same page.
The technical name is an import.
Inside a CLAUDE.md, you write an at sign followed by a path to another file.
For example, @docs/testing-conventions.md.
When Claude Code launches, that referenced file is expanded into context, right alongside the file that references it.
A few precise details.
Four of them.
One.
Relative paths resolve from the importing file, not from the folder you launched in.
Two.
Imports can nest, up to a maximum depth of four hops.
Three.
An at sign inside a code span, meaning the text between backticks, is left alone.
Four.
An import in a project file that points outside the working folder, such as into your home folder, triggers a one-time approval dialog.
The course presenter flagged this as an exam scenario too.
How do you make CLAUDE.md modular?
The import is the mechanism.
His framing was ownership.
The backend team edits the API patterns file.
The testing team edits the testing file.
And the root file stops being a merge-conflict battleground.
Clean pull requests.
Clean ownership.
Question three.
Practice question D3-003.
This one turns on a subtle point.
Here's the scenario.
A platform team's root file holds API patterns, testing conventions, and deployment rules.
Claude genuinely needs all of it, in every session.
Two teams keep colliding in merge conflicts.
They want separate files.
And they accept that total context per session stays the same.
What should they do?
Take a second.
The answer.
Split the sections into topic files, and import each one from the root.
Here's the key line from the notes.
Hold on to it.
Imports organize.
They do not economize.
An imported file still loads at launch.
It still costs the same tokens as if it were pasted inline.
And in this question, that's exactly what the team wants.
Now the wrong turns.
Every other option changes when the content loads.
Wrong: move the sections into rule files with path patterns.
Why?
That makes them conditional.
So guidance needed every session goes missing whenever no matching file is read.
Wrong: move them into subfolder CLAUDE.md files.
Why?
That makes them load on demand.
So they're absent from sessions working elsewhere.
Wrong: convert them into skills.
Why?
That makes them load on demand too.
The deciding phrase is: needed in every session.
Now flip that question around, and the answer flips.
A teammate splits a six-hundred-line CLAUDE.md into eight imported files, and announces the context problem is solved.
Is it?
No.
Startup context is unchanged.
If the goal is a smaller footprint, the tools are conditional loading, meaning path-scoped rules or skills.
Plus deleting anything Claude can work out from the code itself.
And one small freebie from the notes: block-level HTML comments in a CLAUDE.md are stripped before injection.
So maintainer notes cost nothing.
So remember.
An import is for ownership and tidiness.
Never for saving tokens.
And never for conditional loading.
Now the directory level.
Plain version.
Think of an office building where each department tapes its own notice inside its own door.
People read it only when they walk into that department.
And each department updates its sign without asking reception.
In exam terms, you can put a CLAUDE.md inside any subfolder, such as packages/coordinator.
It loads when Claude reads a file there.
Or at launch, if you start Claude in that folder.
Question four.
Practice question D3-004.
Here's the scenario.
A monorepo, meaning one repository holding several packages.
There's a coordinator package, a web-search agent package, and a synthesis agent package.
Each has its own owning team.
Each team wants its conventions in a file right next to its own code, reviewed in its own pull requests.
And when an engineer works only in the coordinator, the web-search conventions should not be in context.
What's the right setup?
Take a second.
The answer.
A CLAUDE.md inside each package directory, owned by that team.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: put all three sections in the root file, under headings like "For packages/web-search-agent/."
Why?
CLAUDE.md has no path-prefix scoping.
Those headings are plain text.
So everything loads, every session.
The course presenter named this one directly: CLAUDE.md with path prefixes does not work.
Wrong: keep a short root file, and import each package's conventions.
Why?
Imports expand at launch.
So everything loads, including during coordinator-only work.
Wrong: central rule files at the root, with a path pattern per package, maintained by a central team.
This is the subtle one.
Why is it wrong?
It does load conditionally.
But it fails on ownership.
The files sit centrally, not beside each team's code.
We'll come back to the rule-versus-directory-file contrast in part three, because it's a favorite.
Hold on to this line.
A subfolder CLAUDE.md loads on demand, and suits teams that own the code beside it.
Last concept in this part.
It ties back to the theme of the cold open.
Question five.
Practice question D3-005.
Here's the scenario.
The project file says: never commit directly to main.
Claude complies early in sessions.
But in long sessions, it has twice committed to main anyway.
The release manager says the rule must hold every single time, for every contributor.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
A hook.
Specifically, a PreToolUse hook.
Here's the plain version.
A sign on the door saying please lock up works most nights.
But not on the night someone is tired.
If the door must be locked every time, you fit a lock that closes itself.
A bigger sign, or one signed by the landlord, is still just a sign.
In exam terms.
Every CLAUDE.md scope, managed policy included, and every rule file, is advisory context.
None of them can block an action.
A PreToolUse hook is a small script Claude Code runs before a tool call.
Here, it checks whether a shell command is a git commit or git push while the current branch is main.
And if so, it refuses it.
The notes call this the enforcement ladder.
Three rungs.
First.
Withhold the capability entirely.
Second.
Deny it in code, with a hook.
Third.
Validate a record afterwards.
A strongly worded sentence is none of the three.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: put it on the first line, in capitals, prefixed with critical.
Why?
It's still advisory prose, competing with the whole context window.
It can be missed, or summarized away, in a long session.
Wrong: ask IT to put it in the managed policy file.
Why?
That file cannot be excluded by individuals, which sounds like enforcement.
But it's still CLAUDE.md content.
Advice Claude weighs.
Not a gate.
Wrong: put it in a rule file whose pattern matches every file, so it reloads constantly.
Why?
A rule is still text.
And reloading text does not stop a commit.
The constraint words are every single time, and must hold.
Those words always point to a hook, or a permission rule.
We'll meet hooks again in part five.
And they're covered in depth in the chapter on agentic architecture.
A few supporting facts round out this task statement.
Three of them.
One.
Keep the root CLAUDE.md short.
Under about two hundred lines.
It should hold only what Claude cannot derive from the code, because a bloated file gets rules ignored.
The notes' test: ask of each line, would removing it cause a mistake?
Two.
There's a setting called claudeMdExcludes.
It skips ancestor CLAUDE.md files by absolute path pattern.
But it cannot exclude the managed policy file.
Why?
Because a policy an individual can erase is not a policy.
Three.
The root project CLAUDE.md is re-read from disk and re-injected after the conversation is compacted.
Subfolder files and path-scoped rules are not.
We'll use that last fact in part three.
Now a contrast segment, because the exam loves routing questions.
Where does a given instruction belong?
Here's the routing, in plain terms.
Six destinations.
One.
A short fact every session needs, like run commands from the package folder.
That goes in the project CLAUDE.md.
Two.
A convention for one file type, like how React components are declared.
That goes in a path-scoped rule.
Three.
Reference material needed only sometimes, like a detailed API response format.
That goes in a skill.
Four.
A side-effecting procedure a human should time, like cutting a release.
That goes in a skill or command that only a human can trigger.
Five.
Something that must never happen, like committing to main.
That goes in a hook.
Six.
Something project-specific but personal, like your sandbox address and your seeded test account.
That goes in CLAUDE.local.md.
And the flip words.
Every contributor, or the pipeline, means project scope.
Only me, in all my projects, means user scope.
Personal, but only for this project, means the local file.
Must hold every time means a hook.
That's part one.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
CLAUDE.md is a shared briefing, not a lock.
Route each instruction by who needs it, and when it should load.
Coming up in part two: custom slash commands and skills.
